summary.text: Oscillation is a repeating variation of some quantity around a central value, such as the swing of a pendulum or the flow of alternating current.
It happens when a system displaced from equilibrium feels a restoring force that pulls it back, while its momentum carries it past the middle again.
Real oscillators lose energy as heat through friction or resistance, so their swings fade unless something keeps feeding them energy.

items.prompt: You pull a toy on a spring downward and let go. It bounces up past its resting height. What carries it past that point?

options.label: The restoring force stays strongest at the middle
Gravity switches direction at the middle
The momentum it gained on the way back
The spring stops pulling at the middle

items.explain: Moving back toward equilibrium gives the mass momentum, which keeps it going past that point and sets up a new restoring force the other way.

items.prompt: A weight hangs from a spring. You then hang a second, heavier load that adds a constant downward pull. What happens to the middle of the bounce?

options.label: It shifts to a new equilibrium point
It stays at the same spot
It disappears and the bouncing stops
It splits into two middle points

items.explain: A constant force such as gravity moves the point of equilibrium, and the oscillation happens around the new point.

items.prompt: A swing is pushed once and then left alone. Over several minutes, its swings get smaller. Which idea explains this best?

options.label: The swing runs out of restoring force
Friction turns some of its energy into heat
The period gets longer and stops it
Its momentum is gradually deleted

items.explain: Real oscillators have dissipative processes that convert stored energy into heat, so oscillations decay unless energy is supplied.

items.prompt: A bridge engineer notes that a perfectly frictionless spring-and-weight model would never stop moving. What property of the model explains that?

options.label: The weight has no momentum
The spring never reaches equilibrium
Gravity keeps adding energy
Nothing removes energy, so the wave never shrinks

items.explain: The cosine describing the motion swings between its positive and negative limits forever, so without friction the system would oscillate indefinitely.

items.prompt: A spring pulls back harder the farther you stretch it. Why is this feature central to oscillation?

options.label: A bigger stretch always returns the mass sooner
A bigger pull cancels out the momentum
A growing pull toward the middle keeps the motion centred on equilibrium
A bigger stretch removes the need for equilibrium

items.explain: Equilibrium plus a restoring force that grows with distance from it are common features of oscillating systems.

items.prompt: A machine's valve flutters rapidly and the control engineers want it to settle. How do they view that oscillation?

options.label: As unwanted, since the aim is a stable state
As ideal, since it shows equilibrium
As a sign of perfect efficiency
As a harmless route to a bigger swing

items.explain: In process control, rapid oscillation can be undesirable because the goal is convergence to a stable state; it is called chattering.

beats.title: Why Things Keep Swinging
beats.hook: A pulled spring never simply stops at the middle, and the reason is hiding in its momentum.

beats.prompt: A mass on a spring is pulled down and released. When it reaches the resting position on the way up, what does it do?
beats.explain: On the way back the mass picked up momentum, so it carries on past equilibrium and a new restoring force builds in the opposite direction.

choices.label: It bounces off the middle like a wall
choices.feedback: Nothing solid is at the middle; only the spring's pull acts on it.

choices.label: It stops there for good
choices.feedback: Tempting, since the spring force is gone at the middle, but the mass is still moving.

choices.label: It keeps moving past the middle

items.label: The mass is displaced from equilibrium
A restoring force pulls it back
A new restoring force acts the opposite way

beats.explain: Displacement creates the restoring force, momentum overshoots, and the overshoot creates a restoring force in the opposite sense.

beats.prompt: Sort each situation by what it shows.
beats.explain: Pendulums and alternating current are familiar examples of oscillation, while chattering and flapping are rapid oscillations that are undesirable in process control.

steps.text: A real spring-mass system loses energy to friction.
That energy is converted into heat.

beats.idea: A restoring force pulls toward equilibrium while momentum carries the system past it, so it swings until energy leaks away.

paragraphs.heading: What oscillation is
paragraphs.text: Oscillation is a repeating, back-and-forth change in some quantity, usually over time, around a central value or between two or more states. The central value is often a point of equilibrium, a resting balance. A swinging pendulum and alternating current are familiar cases. A mechanical oscillation is called a vibration, and physicists also use oscillations to approximate complex interactions, such as those between atoms.

paragraphs.heading: A weight on a spring
paragraphs.text: The simplest mechanical example is a weight on a linear spring, acted on only by its weight and the spring's tension; an air table or ice surface comes close to this. When the spring is still, the system is at equilibrium. Pull the weight aside and a restoring force pushes it back toward equilibrium. By the time it gets there it has picked up momentum, so it overshoots, and a new restoring force builds the other way.

paragraphs.heading: Energy trading places
paragraphs.text: The swinging carries on because energy keeps changing form. As the mass passes equilibrium it has kinetic energy, and at the far ends of its path that energy is stored as potential energy in the spring. When the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement, the regular motion is called simple harmonic motion. The time one oscillation takes is often called its period.

paragraphs.heading: Frequency, amplitude, phase
paragraphs.text: The motion is described by its frequency ω, its amplitude A and a phase shift δ. All three are set by how the system starts out. With no friction, the spring and mass would swing between plus and minus the amplitude forever.

paragraphs.heading: Why swings fade
paragraphs.text: Every real oscillator is thermodynamically irreversible. Friction, electrical resistance and similar processes keep turning some of its stored energy into heat. So oscillations tend to die away unless energy keeps flowing in. With β as the damping coefficient and ω₀ as the natural frequency, damped oscillators fall into three groups. An oscillator is under-damped when β is smaller than ω₀, over-damped when β is larger, and critically damped when the two are equal.

paragraphs.heading: Driving and resonance
paragraphs.text: An oscillator can also be pushed by an outside force, for example an AC circuit hooked up to a power supply outside it; the oscillation is then called driven. Resonance happens in a damped, driven oscillator when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, ω = ω₀. At that point the amplitude of the swings is as large as it can be.

paragraphs.heading: Flutter in a wing
paragraphs.text: Some systems draw energy from their surroundings, usually when they sit in a flowing fluid. Flutter in aircraft wings is an example. A tiny displacement of the wing raises its angle of attack and its lift coefficient, which pushes it still further. At large enough displacements, the wing's stiffness takes over as the restoring force and an oscillation results.

paragraphs.heading: Two directions at once
paragraphs.text: In an anisotropic oscillator the restoring force differs by direction, so each direction has its own frequency. If one frequency is twice the other, the path traces a figure eight. If the ratio of the frequencies is irrational, the motion is quasiperiodic: periodic along each axis, yet it never repeats as a whole.
